questions.q: Why is the first route by which BFS reaches a hub a route with the fewest hops?
questions.explain: A first-in, first-out queue empties layer d before it starts layer d + 1. If a shorter route to a hub existed, the hub would have been discovered in an earlier layer. BFS never tries all routes; it visits each hub once.
options: Because BFS tries every possible route and keeps the shortest
Because the queue processes hubs in layers of increasing distance, so every hub at distance d is discovered before any hub at distance d + 1
Because BFS always follows the neighbour with the smallest name
Because BFS uses recursion

questions.q: What does this BFS print?
questions.explain: Layer 1 is Depot's neighbours in list order: Yaba, Ikeja. Yaba adds Surulere and Ikoyi (layer 2). Ikeja's neighbours are already seen. Ikoyi adds Lekki (layer 3). Ikoyi was discovered from Yaba first, at distance 2.
options:
Depot Yaba Ikeja Surulere Ikoyi Lekki
Depot:0 Yaba:1 Ikeja:1 Surulere:2 Ikoyi:2 Lekki:3

Depot Yaba Surulere Ikoyi Ikeja Lekki
Depot:0 Yaba:1 Surulere:2 Ikoyi:2 Ikeja:1 Lekki:3

Depot Yaba Ikeja Surulere Ikoyi Lekki
Depot:0 Yaba:1 Ikeja:1 Surulere:2 Ikoyi:3 Lekki:4

Depot Ikeja Yaba Ikoyi Surulere Lekki
Depot:0 Ikeja:1 Yaba:1 Ikoyi:2 Surulere:2 Lekki:3

questions.q: Roads have different lengths in km. You run BFS from Lagos and report the route to Abuja as the shortest drive. What is wrong?
questions.explain: BFS treats every edge as cost 1. In the lesson, BFS picked the two-road route through Benin (792 km) while Dijkstra found a three-road route of 758 km.
options: Nothing; BFS finds shortest routes
BFS minimises the number of roads, not the kilometres; a route with more but shorter roads can be shorter to drive. Use Dijkstra for weighted edges
BFS cannot run on undirected graphs
BFS only works when there is exactly one route

questions.q: In BFS, why mark a hub as seen when it is added to the queue rather than when it is taken out?
questions.explain: Both versions give correct distances, but marking late can put a hub in the queue once per neighbour that discovers it. On the open warehouse floor that nearly doubled the queue; on dense graphs it can make it one entry per edge.
options: Marking on take-out gives wrong distances
So every hub enters the queue at most once; marking late lets several neighbours add the same hub before it is processed, filling the queue with duplicates
Because Map entries can only be set once
It makes no difference at all

questions.q: A BFS uses queue.shift() to take the next hub. On a graph with a million vertices it is very slow. Why?
questions.explain: Removing from the front of an array shifts the rest. Reading queue[head++] leaves the array alone and costs O(1), keeping BFS at O(V + E).
options: shift returns items in the wrong order
shift moves every remaining element one place left, O(n) per call, so the search becomes O(V²); use a head index or a real queue
Arrays cannot hold a million items
BFS is always O(V²)

questions.q: BFS gives you each hub's distance. How do you recover the actual route to a destination?
questions.explain: Parent links cost O(V) memory in total. Walking back from the goal takes one step per hop. Storing full routes in the queue would copy paths and cost far more memory.
options: Run BFS again from the destination
Sort the hubs by distance
When a hub is discovered, store the hub it was reached from (its parent); follow parents back from the destination to the start and reverse
Store the entire route for every hub in the queue

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: Following parents from Abuja gives Abuja, Ilorin, Ibadan, Lagos; reversing puts the start first. The start's parent is null, so its route is just itself. A hub with no parent entry was never reached: null.
options:
Lagos > Ibadan > Ilorin > Abuja
Lagos
null

Abuja > Ilorin > Ibadan > Lagos
Lagos
null

Lagos > Ibadan > Ilorin > Abuja

null

Lagos > Ibadan > Ilorin > Abuja
Lagos
[]

questions.q: What should a route finder do when asked for a route to a hub that exists but cannot be reached, and when asked for a hub name that does not exist ("Maidugri")?
questions.explain: "We do not deliver there" is a normal answer the caller can show. A misspelt hub is a bug or bad input; failing loudly with the name in the message makes it easy to find. Treating them the same hides typos.
options: Throw an error in both cases
Return null in both cases
Return null (a valid "no route" answer) for the unreachable hub, and throw for the unknown name, which is bad input
Return an empty route in both cases

questions.q: BFS on an undirected graph with 17 hubs and 20 routes made 40 neighbour checks. What is its complexity in general?
questions.explain: Each hub is processed once (V), and processing a hub scans its adjacency list. Across all hubs the lists hold 2E entries for an undirected graph. Total O(V + E).
options: O(V²)
O(V log V)
O(V + E): each vertex is taken from the queue once and each undirected edge is looked at twice, once from each end
O(E²)

questions.q: Which statement about depth-first search is true?
questions.explain: DFS goes as deep as it can along whichever neighbour comes first. It is ideal for reachability, components, cycle detection and topological order, but not for shortest paths.
options: DFS finds shortest routes, but more slowly than BFS
DFS reaches every vertex BFS reaches, in O(V + E), but the routes it follows are not necessarily shortest
DFS only works on trees
DFS visits vertices in order of distance from the start

questions.q: What does this recursive DFS print?
questions.explain: From Yaba, DFS goes to Surulere (dead end, back up), then Ikoyi. Ikoyi's first unseen neighbour is Ikeja, visited before Lekki. Compare with BFS on the same graph, which visits Ikeja second.
options: Depot Yaba Surulere Ikoyi Ikeja Lekki
Depot Yaba Ikeja Surulere Ikoyi Lekki
Depot Yaba Surulere Ikoyi Lekki Ikeja
Depot Ikeja Ikoyi Lekki Yaba Surulere

questions.q: An iterative DFS pushes all unseen neighbours and pops the newest. What does it print?
questions.explain: A pushes B then C; C is popped first (newest). C pushes D. D is popped next; its neighbours are already seen. Finally B. With a queue (oldest first) the order would be A B C D.
options: A C D B
A B D C
A B C D
A C B D

questions.q: A recursive DFS over a referral chain of 100,000 customers throws RangeError: Maximum call stack size exceeded. What is the proper fix?
questions.explain: Every nested call uses a frame on the limited call stack. An array lives on the heap and can hold millions of entries. The search logic is unchanged: pop, visit, push unseen neighbours. (BFS would also work, but not with shift.)
options: Catch the error and return a partial result
Increase the size of the Set
Use an explicit stack (an array you push to and pop from) instead of recursion, so the depth is limited only by memory
Switch to BFS with shift()

questions.q: An iterative DFS and a BFS written with an array differ in essentially one line. Which?
questions.explain: Both keep a collection of discovered but unprocessed vertices. Taking the newest gives depth-first order; taking the oldest gives layers. Swapping in a priority queue ordered by distance gives Dijkstra.
options: The visited check
Which end the next vertex is taken from: the newest (pop, a stack) for DFS, the oldest (queue[head++]) for BFS
DFS uses a Map, BFS a Set
DFS starts from the goal instead of the start

questions.q: A warehouse floor is a grid of 200 × 300 cells. How does BFS for the robot's shortest route treat it?
questions.explain: You do not need to materialise the graph. Each cell has at most four neighbours, so E is at most about 4V, and BFS is linear in the number of cells. Grids have lots of cycles, which is why the seen set is essential.
options: First convert it into a Map with 60,000 keys and their neighbour lists
Each free cell is a vertex; its neighbours are computed on the fly from row and column (up, down, left, right) with a bounds and wall check; the cost is O(rows × columns)
Grids need a different algorithm than graphs
Use DFS, because grids have no cycles

questions.q: What does this grid BFS print?
questions.explain: The shortest route is (0,0) → (1,0) → (1,1) → (2,1) → (2,2): 4 moves. Diagonal moves are not allowed, so it cannot be 3. Of the 9 cells, 3 are walls, so BFS reaches the other 6.
options: undefined 6

questions.q: After floods close some roads, how do you find all groups of hubs that can still reach each other?
questions.explain: One search only finds the group containing its start. Starting a new search from every unvisited hub finds every group, and because the seen set is shared, each vertex and edge is still handled once overall.
options: Run one BFS from Lagos
Loop over all hubs; start a BFS or DFS from each hub not yet seen; everything that search reaches is one group. O(V + E) in total
Run Dijkstra from every hub
Sort the hubs by name and group neighbours

questions.q: What does this print?
questions.explain: A–B–C form one group and D–E another. F has only a road to itself, so it is a group of one. G has no roads at all but is still a hub, and it only appears because the graph was built from the hub list, not from the roads.

questions.q: A report of cut-off areas builds its graph only from the roads that are still open. Which hubs can it silently leave out?
questions.explain: A graph built from edges only contains vertices that appear in an edge. A hub whose roads are all closed disappears from the map and from the report. Create the vertices from the list of hubs first.
options: Hubs with the most roads
Hubs that have no open road left, which are exactly the most cut-off ones
Hubs whose names come last alphabetically
None; every hub appears in some road

questions.q: A connected group of 8 hubs has 8 roads (undirected, no duplicates). What can you conclude?
questions.explain: A connected graph with V vertices needs at least V − 1 edges, and with exactly V − 1 it is a tree. Each edge beyond that creates one independent cycle. 8 edges on 8 vertices means one cycle.
options: It has no cycle; it is a tree
It has exactly one cycle, so one road can close without splitting the group
It is disconnected
Nothing without running DFS

questions.q: Transfers: Ada → Bola, Ada → Chidi, Bola → Chidi. A DFS from Ada meets Chidi a second time. Is that a circular transfer?
questions.explain: In a directed graph, reaching an already-seen vertex is normal. The three-colour rule separates "finished" (black) from "on the current path" (grey). Only a grey target closes a loop back to where the money came from.
options: Yes, meeting a visited account always means a cycle
No; Chidi is already finished (black) when reached again, which just means two paths lead there. Only an edge back to an account still on the current path (grey) is a cycle
Yes, because Chidi receives money twice
It depends on the amounts

questions.q: What does this cycle check print?
questions.explain: In the diamond, D is black when reached the second time: no cycle. A → B → C → A returns to a grey vertex. A transfer from an account to itself is a cycle of length one: A is grey when its own edge is checked.
options: false true true
true true true
false true false
true true false

questions.q: Why is a city's distance final the first time Dijkstra takes it out of the priority queue?
questions.explain: This is the BFS layer argument with distances. It depends on non-negative weights: any detour through a waiting city adds a non-negative amount to a distance that is already at least as large.
options: Because each city is only pushed once
Every entry still in the queue is at least as far, and roads have non-negative lengths, so no route through them can be shorter
Because the heap is sorted
Because Dijkstra checks all routes before popping

questions.q: A route earns the driver a rebate, modelled as a negative cost of −₦4,000. What happens with Dijkstra?
questions.explain: Dijkstra's correctness argument needs non-negative weights. The lesson's version throws a RangeError on a negative length instead of returning a silently wrong route. Bellman-Ford handles negative weights in O(V × E).
options: It works, because the costs still add up
It loops forever
It can return a wrong answer: a city is finalised when popped, and a negative edge found later could make it cheaper, but Dijkstra never revisits it
JavaScript throws when adding a negative number

questions.q: When Dijkstra finds a shorter route to a city that is already in the heap, the lesson's code pushes a new entry instead of updating the old one. How are the old entries handled?
questions.explain: A binary heap cannot find an arbitrary entry quickly, so updating is awkward. Pushing a new entry and ignoring stale ones (lazy deletion) is simple; the heap holds at most one entry per edge.
options: They are removed from the heap immediately
They stay in the heap and are skipped when popped, because the city is already in the done set
They cause wrong distances
The heap overwrites them automatically

questions.q: What is the cost of Dijkstra with a binary heap on a graph with V cities and E roads?
questions.explain: Each edge can cause one push and each entry one pop, each O(log E) = O(log V). BFS saves the log factor because a plain queue is O(1), which only works when every edge costs the same.
options: O(V + E)
O((V + E) log V)
O(V²E)
O(2<sup>V</sup>)

questions.q: What does this simple Dijkstra (scanning for the closest unfinished city) print?
questions.explain: C is closest (1). From C, B improves to 1 + 2 = 3 and D becomes 9. B (3) is next and improves D to 3 + 5 = 8. This array-scanning version is O(V²), fine for small or dense graphs.

questions.q: Why do map applications use A* instead of plain Dijkstra for a route from Lagos to Kano?
questions.explain: With a good estimate (such as straight-line distance, which never overestimates), A* returns the same shortest route while expanding far fewer junctions.
options: A* allows negative road lengths
Dijkstra cannot handle more than a thousand junctions
Dijkstra expands in all directions, including away from Kano; A* adds an estimate of the remaining distance to each priority, so the search leans towards the goal and explores far less
A* finds shorter routes than Dijkstra

questions.q: For every street in a town you need the distance to the nearest of 12 parcel lockers. What is the efficient approach?
questions.explain: With all sources in the first layer, the ripples spread together and each street is claimed by the nearest locker first. That is one O(V + E) search instead of twelve (or one per street).
options: Run one BFS per street
Run one BFS per locker and take the minimum at each street: 12 searches
One BFS that starts with all 12 lockers in the queue at distance 0 (multi-source BFS)
Dijkstra from the town centre

questions.q: A "people you may know" feature searches the follow graph of a social network with 50 million accounts. What is essential?
questions.explain: BFS layers grow very fast on social graphs. Suggestions only need friends of friends, so a depth limit bounds the work, and a visit cap and timeout protect the server.
options: Use DFS so it finishes faster
Limit the depth (for example to 2 hops) and the number of accounts visited, so a request from a popular account cannot explore most of the database
Load the whole graph into memory first
Use Dijkstra with all weights 1

questions.q: Which statement about memory use is right?
questions.explain: On a wide, shallow graph (social networks) BFS's frontier can be huge while DFS's path stays short. On a long chain it is the other way round. Both use O(V) in the worst case for the seen set.
options: BFS and DFS always use the same memory
BFS holds a whole layer in its queue, which can be very wide; DFS holds the current path, which can be very deep
DFS always uses more memory than BFS
BFS uses no memory beyond the graph

questions.q: This walk forgets the seen set. A safety cap stops it. What does it print?
questions.explain: Every hub pushes its neighbours again, including the one it came from, so the walk bounces between hubs forever. Only the cap stops it, and the queue keeps growing faster than it is consumed. Every graph walk needs a seen set.
options: 1000 true
3 false
1000 false
4 true

questions.q: Write hops(graph, start, goal) that returns the fewest number of routes between two hubs with BFS, 0 if they are the same hub, and -1 if the goal cannot be reached. It should print 2 0 -1 3.
questions.explain: Checking hub === goal when a hub is taken out handles start equals goal (distance 0) and stops early. If the queue empties without reaching the goal, it is unreachable.

questions.q: Extend BFS to return the route itself: record each hub's parent when it is discovered, then walk back from the goal. Return null when unreachable. It should print Depot > Yaba > Ikoyi > Lekki and then null.
questions.explain: The parent map doubles as the seen set. Ikoyi is discovered first from Yaba (Yaba comes before Ikeja in the queue), so the route goes through Yaba. Epe has no parent entry: unreachable.

questions.q: Count the connected groups of hubs. Build the graph from the hub list (so hubs without roads count as their own group), then start a search from every hub not yet seen. It should print 3.
questions.explain: Lagos–Ibadan, Kano–Kaduna and Calabar alone. Any search works for components; this one is an iterative DFS. Building from the hub list is what makes Calabar count.

questions.q: Write steps(rows): the fewest moves (up, down, left, right) from S to E, never entering #, or -1 if impossible. It should print 6 and then -1.
questions.explain: The wall in column 2 forces the robot down to row 2: (0,0) → (1,0) → (1,1) → (2,1) → (2,2) → (2,3) → (1,3) is 6 moves. In the second map the wall blocks the only way, so the queue empties and the answer is -1. Check bounds before reading the grid; a cell outside the map has no row to read.

questions.q: A banquet hall seat map shows free seats (.) and taken ones (x). Guests at a table count as sitting together if their seats are adjacent up, down, left or right. Find the size of the largest block of connected free seats (a flood fill). It should print 6.
questions.explain: This is connected components on a grid. The right block has 6 seats: (0,3), (0,4), (1,4), (2,3), (2,4) and (3,4). The left block has 5, and the free seat in row 3, column 2 is on its own because all its neighbours are taken. Each seat is pushed once, so the flood fill is O(rows × columns).

questions.q: Write cheapest(roads, start): Dijkstra with a simple scan for the closest unfinished city (no heap needed for a handful of cities). roads maps each city to an object of neighbour costs in naira. It should print Ibadan 7500 Ilorin 17000 Abuja 45000 Benin 19000.
questions.explain: Abuja costs 45,000 through Ibadan and Ilorin, against 49,000 through Benin. Scanning all cities for the closest one is O(V) per step, O(V²) in total: simple, and fine when V is small. For large sparse graphs use the heap version.

questions.q: Write circular(transfers) that returns true if the directed transfers contain a loop, using DFS with three states (unvisited, on the current path, finished). It should print false true.
questions.explain: In the first list Chidi is reached twice, but when it is reached the second time it is already finished. In the second, Dayo → Bola points back to an account still on the current path. The outer loop starts a search from every account, so loops that Ada cannot reach are found too.

questions.q: This BFS never expands hubs at the depth limit. What does it print?
questions.explain: Hubs at distance 2 (Ilorin, Onitsha) are discovered, so they get a distance, but never expanded, so Abuja and Enugu are never reached. Only Lagos, Ibadan and Benin are expanded.
options: Lagos Ibadan Benin Ilorin Onitsha 3
Lagos Ibadan Benin Ilorin Onitsha Abuja Enugu 5
Lagos Ibadan Benin 1
Lagos Ibadan Benin Ilorin Onitsha 5

questions.q: A street has lockers at positions 0 and 7. A single BFS starts from both. What does it print?
questions.explain: Both lockers start at distance 0, so the ripples spread from both ends at once and each house takes the distance of the nearer locker. House 4 is 4 from locker 0 but 3 from locker 7, so it gets 3.

questions.q: This Dijkstra uses a sorted array as its priority queue and lazy deletion. What does it print?
questions.explain: B is first pushed at 10 (from A), then again at 3 (through C). The entry at 3 comes out first and B is finalised; D becomes 4. The stale entry ["B", 10] is popped later and skipped: 5 pops for 4 cities.
